systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : JNS.org
Rubrique : Sanctions et export
Date du flux : 10/11/2026
Auteur : JNS Staff
Titre d'origine : France to summon Iranian envoy, seek EU sanctions over cyberattack

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (JNS.org) :
The French government is ruling out “nothing” in responding to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators that Paris has blamed on Iran, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday, AFP reported.
Barrot told Franceinfo that Iran’s ambassador will be summoned and that Paris will seek European sanctions against the Islamic regime. He said his government will take all measures “that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” including “those we may not disclose publicly.”
The goal, he said, is “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again.”
On Monday, France accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of carrying out the attack last month, which made fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heat up. Millions of euros’ worth of food spoiled, and fires broke out in some stores.
Barrot called the attack “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression.”
Media reports have suggested similar cyberattacks may also have hit stores in other European countries.
Les 11 et 12 octobre, près de 700 sites de distribution ont été touchés par une campagne cyber d'une ampleur et d’une agressivité inédites.
Aujourd’hui, grâce au travail des services de l’Etat, nous connaissons les responsables : les Gardiens de la Révolution de la République… pic.twitter.com/7KQru9as9x
— Jean-Noël Barrot (@jnbarrot) November 9, 2026

SOURCE 2 (Ticker News) :
France summons Iran’s ambassador over cyberattack on supermarkets, threatens sanctions and response measures against Tehran
France summoned Iran’s ambassador, accusing Tehran of a cyberattack disabling refrigerators in supermarkets, with Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot warning of potential cyber countermeasures.
Officials claimed Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind the October attacks affecting refrigeration systems across France.
The Iranian foreign ministry called these accusations “baseless and hostile.”
France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed the ambassador’s summoning took place on Tuesday.
Cyber response
Barrot indicated France might pursue EU sanctions, describing the attack as unprecedented.
He suggested undisclosed actions may follow.
France will take proportional measures deemed necessary to prevent future attacks and penalize responsible parties.
Barrot highlighted France’s cyberdefence options available to authorities.
The supermarket cyberattacks were among the most disruptive since the Iran conflict began, alongside attacks on the Los Angeles transit system and U.S. water plants.
Iran routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks.
Paris and Tehran relations have been tense due to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, regional activities, and the detention of French nationals.
Relations briefly improved but soured again after diplomatic expulsions over the summer.
French officials cite Tehran’s hostility over France’s support for Iranian civil society.

SOURCE 3 (Hindustan Times) :
France summons Iran envoy over cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators, warns of retaliation
French officials on Monday accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of orchestrating the attacks
France summoned Iran's ambassador on Tuesday over an alleged cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets across the country, with foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot warning that Paris could retaliate with cyber measures of its own.
French officials on Monday accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of orchestrating the attacks, which affected commercial refrigeration systems across France in October, according to Reuters.
The French foreign ministry reportedly said the Iranian ambassador, whose summoning had been announced a day earlier by Barrot, was called in on Tuesday morning.
Also Read | France blames Iran for ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack on fridges, launches probe and vows sanctions
Speaking to France Info television, as cited by Reuters, Barrot called the incident an "attack of unprecedented scale and aggression" on French soil and said Paris would push for EU sanctions against Tehran in response.
He said there could be further action that would not be disclosed.
"We will take whatever measures are necessary, including some that we will not discuss publicly, if we judge them proportionate and necessary to deter any new attacks and punish those responsible for this unacceptable aggression," Barrot said and added France's cyberdefence doctrine provided authorities with a range of options.
According to AFP, the cyberattacks targeted 700 sites, with hackers gaining control of cooling systems through web interfaces to trigger "abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles". They also disabled sensor alerts designed to warn operators when temperatures crossed a specified threshold.
Also Read | Not Russia this time? France blames IRGC for European supermarket cyberattacks; Germany backs Paris
Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.
On November 2, stores in at least nine other European countries were hit by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems.
Relations between Paris and Tehran have been strained for years over Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, its regional activities and the detention of several French nationals. Tensions have also been fuelled by French allegations that Iran has spread misinformation linked to protests that have rocked France over the past month.
Iran's mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment on Monday, said Reuters.
A cyber unit linked to IRGC behind the cyberattacks?
Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that an investigation had been opened into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), over the attacks, according to AFP. Her office has also sought international arrest warrants against two officials associated with the unit.
Beccuau described Shahid Kaveh as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Centre of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-CEC)".
France's Centre for Coordination of Cyber Crises, which brings together security agencies, including intelligence services, said the unit conducts large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for sabotage. Its operations are directed primarily against Israel and the United States, but also target France and other European countries, the centre said.
(With Reuters and AFP inputs)
